followUps:
A change to transform skips style recalculation of geometry, layout and paint; only the composite step runs.

The element must already sit on its own layer. The GPU then re-stacks the cached texture with a new matrix, so even a busy main thread does not stall it. Changing left instead runs style, layout, paint and composite every frame.

The preload scanner is a second, lightweight parser that races ahead of the main HTML parser to start downloads early. It cannot see resources that only exist after code runs.

It finds <img>, <link> and <script src> in the markup. It misses CSS background-image, images chosen by JavaScript, fonts referenced only inside CSS files, and anything injected by client-side rendering.

CSS blocks rendering; JavaScript blocks the parser. CSS stops first paint until the CSSOM is built, but the parser keeps reading HTML.

A plain <script> stops HTML parsing while it downloads and runs, and it also waits for any CSS above it, because scripts may read styles. defer and async remove the parser blocking; media-query CSS such as media="print" is not render-blocking.

Because layout is relational: a box's size and position depend on its parent, siblings and children.

If a block grows from 100px to 150px, every sibling below it moves down 50px, and a parent with auto height grows too. Browsers try to limit the dirty area, but one change near the top of a flow can re-lay-out most of the page. Absolute-positioned or contain: layout elements limit the spread.

Turn on Paint flashing in the Rendering drawer, and use the Performance panel for exact costs.

  1. Open DevTools, then More tools, then Rendering.
  2. Tick Paint flashing: repainted regions flash green.
  3. Tick Layout Shift Regions or use Layers to see compositor layers.
  4. Record in Performance and look for purple (Layout) and green (Paint) bars.

No. Both hide the element, but display: none removes it from the render tree, while opacity: 0 keeps it.

With display: none the box takes no space and costs no layout or paint, and toggling it causes a reflow. With opacity: 0 the box still takes space, still takes clicks, is still laid out, but needs no paint of its own, and animating it is compositor-only. visibility: hidden sits in between: space kept, repaint only.

code.title: Layout thrashing: interleaved vs batched reads and writes

followUps:
Anything that returns geometry or computed layout makes the browser flush pending style and layout work first.

Common ones: offsetWidth/Height/Top/Left, clientWidth/Height, scrollTop/Height, getBoundingClientRect(), getComputedStyle(el).width and innerHeight. Methods like scrollIntoView() and focus() can also force it. Reads are cheap only when layout is already clean.

Look for purple Layout bars marked with a red triangle and the warning "Forced reflow" in the Performance panel.

Record a trace, open the Main thread flame chart, and zoom on a long task. A repeating pattern of tiny script blocks each followed by a purple Layout block means thrashing. Click the Layout event: the call stack and the Summary show which line triggered it. The Bottom-Up tab also totals time per function.

Usually not, because it runs after React has written to the DOM but before the browser paints, which is exactly the right place to measure once.

It becomes a problem if you read layout in many components or in a loop, or write and then read repeatedly: each read after a write forces a reflow, and the first paint is delayed. Keep one measurement per commit, batch reads before writes, and prefer ResizeObserver when a size only needs to be watched.

code.title: Why Core Web Vitals use p75, not the mean

followUps:
Because averages are dragged by a few extreme values, while p75 describes what most users actually experience.

With ten LCP times, 1.2 to 2.2 seconds for eight visits and 6 and 9 for two, the mean is 2.8 s but the 75th percentile is 2.2 s. The p75 still keeps the slow tail visible: a page passes only when at least 75 percent of visits are good. Median would hide a quarter of users.

INP replaced First Input Delay (FID) in March 2024, because FID measured too little.

FID only timed the delay before the browser started handling the first interaction. It ignored handler time, the time to the next paint, and every later interaction. INP observes all clicks, taps and key presses during the visit and reports roughly the worst one (to ignore outliers on very long visits), from input to next paint, so it reflects the real feeling of responsiveness.

Lab data comes from a controlled test run; field data comes from real users' browsers.

Lab (Lighthouse, WebPageTest) is repeatable and lets you debug with throttling and traces, but it uses one device, one network and no real interactions. Field data (CrUX, your own RUM) shows true p75 across devices, countries and sessions, and is what Google uses for ranking signals, but it is noisy and tells you less about the cause. Use field to find problems, lab to fix them.

preload says "fetch this resource early because this page needs it"; fetchpriority says "when you fetch it, rank it higher or lower".

An <img> in the HTML is already discovered by the scanner, so adding fetchpriority="high" is often enough: it moves the image ahead of other requests. preload is for resources the scanner cannot see (CSS background, font, JS-chosen image), and it can combine with fetchpriority too.

Because the browser only discovers a CSS background after it has downloaded and parsed the CSS and matched the element, so the image request starts late.

An <img src> is found by the preload scanner in the first bytes of HTML. A background image waits for the CSS file (render-blocking), then CSSOM, then the request. That adds one whole round trip to LCP and gives no srcset, loading or fetchpriority control.

SSR usually improves LCP, because the HTML already contains the content and the preload scanner can see the hero image straight away.

With client-only rendering the browser must download, parse and run the JS bundle before any element exists, so LCP waits for all of it. SSR trades this for a possibly higher TTFB (the server renders first), so use streaming, caching or edge rendering. Hydration still costs INP, so SSR helps LCP more than interactivity.

code.title: Computing a layout shift score

followUps:
Each shift scores impact fraction x distance fraction.

Impact fraction is the share of the viewport covered by the unstable element before and after the move. Distance fraction is the largest move, divided by the larger viewport dimension. Example: a 400x200 box in a 400x800 viewport moves down 100px. Impact is 120000 / 320000 = 0.375, distance is 100 / 800 = 0.125, score is 0.047. All shifts are then summed.

A session window groups layout shifts so CLS measures the worst burst, not the whole visit.

A window starts at the first shift and ends when there is a 1 second gap with no shifts or after 5 seconds total. Shifts inside a window are added, and the page's CLS is the largest window. That keeps a long-lived page, such as a single-page app open for an hour, from being penalised for tiny shifts that add up.

Collect shift data with the web-vitals library's attribution build or a PerformanceObserver for layout-shift entries.

Each entry has sources with the node, its previous rect and its current rect. Send the largest source's CSS selector, the score, page route and device type to your RUM backend, and group by selector. You then see, for example, that .promo-banner causes 60 percent of all CLS.

code.title: Virtualized list window and clamping

followUps:
Store a height for each row, accumulate them into prefix sums, and use binary search on scroll position to find the first visible row.

Unmeasured rows use an estimate (say 50px); once a row renders you measure it with ResizeObserver and update the sums. Example: heights 40, 60, 40 give offsets 0, 40, 100, 140; scrollTop 90 lands in row 1. Lookup is O(log n); an update is O(n) naive or O(log n) with a Fenwick tree. Adjust scroll to avoid jumps when rows above change.

Virtualize both axes independently: compute a visible row range and a visible column range, and render only their intersection.

Each cell is positioned with translate(colOffset, rowOffset) inside a spacer of total width and height. Frozen header rows or columns are rendered separately and sticky. With 10,000 rows and 50 columns, a 600x1200 viewport draws about 15 x 12 = 180 cells, not 500,000. Column widths can use prefix sums too.

Do not virtualize when the list is short or when native behaviour matters more than DOM size.

Under a few hundred simple rows the extra code, scroll jank and edge cases cost more than they save. Native features break with virtualization: Ctrl+F, text selection across rows, accessibility navigation, print, and anchor links. Prefer pagination, content-visibility: auto, or a lighter row first, and measure before adding it.

code.title: Debounce with trailing and leading modes

followUps:
Throttle with a timestamp and a timer: run immediately if enough time has passed (leading), and remember the latest arguments to run once more at the end of the interval (trailing).

function throttle(fn, ms) {
  let last = 0, t = null, lastArgs;
  return (...a) => { lastArgs = a; const left = ms - (Date.now() - last);
    if (left <= 0) { last = Date.now(); fn(...a); }
    else if (!t) t = setTimeout(() => { t = null; last = Date.now(); fn(...lastArgs); }, left); };
}

Replace the real clock with a fake one so tests run instantly and deterministically.

With Jest or Vitest call useFakeTimers(), call the debounced function three times, assert the spy was not called, then advanceTimersByTime(wait) and assert it ran once with the last arguments. Also test cancel(), a second burst after the wait, and that throttle fires at 0 ms and at the interval end. Remember to restore real timers after each test.

You get a brand-new debounced function on every render, each with its own timer, so nothing is debounced at all.

Typing "abc" re-renders three times; each render makes a fresh closure with no shared timer, so every keystroke fires the call after the wait. Worse, old timers fire after unmount. Create it once with useMemo or useRef (reading the latest callback through a ref) and call cancel() in the effect cleanup.

Preload says "I need this now, fetch it at high priority"; prefetch says "I might need this later, fetch it when idle".

<link rel="preload" as="script"> is for the current page's critical files, and the browser warns if they go unused. rel="prefetch" loads next-route chunks at lowest priority and keeps them in cache. modulepreload is the version for ES modules, which also parses the module and its imports.

A chunk load error means the browser failed to fetch a split JS file, typically after a new deploy removed the old hashed file or the network dropped.

Handle it by catching the rejected import(), retrying once or twice with backoff, and if it still fails, showing a "reload" prompt or doing one guarded location.reload(). Prevent it by keeping old assets on the CDN for a while after deploy and by wrapping lazy routes in an error boundary.

No. Splitting usually adds some bytes, but each user downloads fewer bytes up front, which is the goal.

Each chunk repeats module wrappers and may duplicate shared code if the split is poor. A single 300 KB bundle might become three chunks totalling 310 KB, yet the first page needs only 120 KB. Total bytes can even grow, so judge by what the first route needs and by cache reuse across routes, using a bundle analyzer.

code.title: Picking an image from srcset and sizes

followUps:
Without sizes, the browser assumes the image slot is the full viewport width (100vw), so it often downloads a bigger file than needed.

On a 1200px wide screen with a 400px-wide image slot, it needs 1200 pixels but you only needed 400, so it picks a 1280px file instead of 640px, wasting several times the bytes. With sizes="400px" (or a media-query list) it can match the real slot. sizes must be accurate, since the browser decides before CSS layout.

Art direction is needed when you want a different crop or composition at different sizes, not just a smaller copy of the same picture.

Example: a wide hero banner on desktop and a tightly cropped portrait of the subject's face on a phone. Use <picture> with <source media="(max-width: 600px)" srcset="hero-narrow.jpg">. For the same picture at different resolutions, plain srcset with sizes is enough, and the format switch uses type.

They normalise the URL or the cache key, so there are only a few variants per image instead of one per tiny parameter change.

Use a fixed set of widths (320, 640, 960, 1280) rather than any pixel width, round the DPR, and limit quality values. When format is negotiated through the Accept header, add Vary: Accept (or the CDN's equivalent), so AVIF, WebP and JPEG are cached separately and each served correctly. A limited set raises the cache hit rate.

The browser creates a layer when it must animate or isolate the element on the GPU.

Triggers: will-change: transform/opacity, a 3D transform such as translateZ(0), an active transform or opacity animation, <video> and <canvas>, position: fixed in many browsers, and elements that overlap an existing layer (implicit promotion). Each layer uses GPU memory, so create them deliberately.

Because box-shadow is painted by the CPU into the layer, so animating it repaints every frame, and big blurred shadows are expensive to rasterise.

A shadow with a 40px blur on a large card means many pixels per frame. A cheaper trick is to put the final shadow on a pseudo-element and animate only its opacity, which is compositor-only. The same advice applies to filter and border-radius changes.

The time budget per frame shrinks from about 16.7 ms to about 8.3 ms.

At 60 Hz, 1000 / 60 = 16.7 ms; at 120 Hz, 1000 / 120 = 8.3 ms for JavaScript, style, layout, paint and composite together. Work that comfortably fits at 60 Hz may drop frames at 120 Hz. This makes compositor-only animations and short tasks (under 50 ms, ideally much less) even more important.

CrUX (Chrome User Experience Report) is a public dataset of real-user metrics collected from opted-in Chrome users, aggregated per origin and URL over a rolling 28 days.

Its limits: Chrome only (no Safari or Firefox), a minimum traffic threshold so small pages have no data, a 28-day lag that delays seeing a fix, and no per-session detail or logged-in pages. Use your own RUM for debugging and finer segments.

Use the web-vitals library's attribution build, which reports the interaction target and the phases of the slowest interaction.

It splits INP into input delay, processing time and presentation delay, and tells you the element selector and event type. If processing time dominates, the handler is the issue, and the Long Animation Frames API (LoAF) names the script, function and source line. Send these fields to your RUM backend and group by selector.

Third-party scripts run on the same main thread but out of your control, and on real devices they vary far more than in the lab.

Consent banners, ads, A/B tools and chat widgets add long tasks that block input (hurting INP) and inject content late (hurting CLS and LCP). A low-end phone may run a 50 ms script in 300 ms. In Lighthouse they often appear small because they load under ideal conditions. Load them with async or defer, delay until idle, and reserve their space.

Save the scroll position and the loaded data before navigating, and restore both on return; the browser's back/forward cache (bfcache) can restore the whole page for free.

Make the page bfcache-eligible (no unload handlers, no open connections). For single-page apps, keep the pages and cursor in a store or history.state, store scrollY on leave, and after rendering enough rows, call scrollTo. With virtualization, restore the offset and measure rows first.

Insert them without moving what the user is reading: show a "3 new posts" button instead of pushing content down automatically.

If the user is already at the top, prepending is fine. Otherwise keep their position by adding the new items' height to scrollTop (or rely on CSS scroll anchoring, overflow-anchor), and use stable keys so existing rows are not re-rendered. This also prevents layout shift.

Measure what the user feels and what the browser pays: INP, scroll smoothness, memory and DOM size, plus loading speed of each new page.

Examples: INP p75 under 200 ms after 1,000 items, frame rate during scroll above 55 fps, DOM nodes below about 1,500, heap growth under a set limit, time to load the next page after the sentinel is hit, and error and retry rates. Use RUM bucketed by items scrolled (10, 100, 1,000) to see degradation.
